cor-basis-existence.title: Existence of Basis
cor-basis-existence.html: Every finite spanning set of a vector space \(V\) contains a basis.

def-additive-inverse-notation.title: Notation of Additive Inverse
def-additive-inverse-notation.html: The unique inverse of a vector \(\v \in V\), for a vector space \(V\) over \(F\), will be denoted as \(-\v\).

def-basis.title: Basis
def-basis.html:
A subset \(B\) of a vector space \(V\) is called a basis for \(V\) if:

  1. \(B\) is linearly independent;
  2. \(B\) spans \(V\).

def-coordinates.title: Coordinates
def-coordinates.html: Let \(B = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \}\) be an ordered basis for \(V\). For any \(\v \in V\), the unique scalars \(c_1, \dots, c_n\) such that \(\v = \sum c_i \v_i\) are called the coordinates of \(\v\) with respect to \(B\). We write this as a column vector: \[ [\v]_B = \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{bmatrix}. \]

def-dimension.title: Dimension
def-dimension.html: A vector space \(V\) over \(F\) is called finite-dimensional if it has a finite basis. The dimension of \(V\), denoted \(\dim_F (V)\), is the number of vectors in any basis for \(V\). By convention, \(\dim_F (\{\mathbf{0}\}) = 0\).

def-direct-sum.title: Direct Sum of Two Subspaces
def-direct-sum.html: Let \(W_1\), \(W_2\) be subspaces of a vector space \(V\). If \(W_1 \cap W_2 = \{ \mathbf{0} \}\), then we write \(W_1 + W2\) as \[ W_1 \oplus W_2 \] and call it the direct sum of \(W_1\) and \(W_2\).

def-linear-combination.title: Linear Combination
def-linear-combination.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\), \(S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_m \}\) be a subset of \(V\). Then the expression \[ a_1 \v_1 + a_2 \v_2 + \cdots + a_m \v_m \] is called a linear combination of \(S\). The scalars \(a_i\) are called the coefficients of the linear combination.

def-linear-independence.title: Linear Independence
def-linear-independence.html:
A subset \(S\) of a vector space \(V\) is said to be linearly independent if for any distinct vectors \(\v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n \in S\), the only solution to the equation: \[ a_1 \v_1 + a_2 \v_2 + \dots + a_n \v_n = \mathbf{0} \] is the trivial solution \(a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_n = 0\).

If there exists a non-trivial solution (where at least one \(a_i \neq 0\)), then \(S\) is said to be linearly dependent.

def-span.title: Span
def-span.html:
Let \(S\) be a subset of a vector space \(V\) over \(F\). The span of \(S\), denoted by \(\Span_F(S)\), is the set of all linear combinations of finite subsets of elements of \(S\).

If \(S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n \}\), then \(\Span_F(S) = \{ a_1 \v_1 + a_2 \v_2 + \dots + a_n \v_n : a_i \in F \}\). By convention, \(\Span_F(\varnothing) = \{ \mathbf{0} \}\).

def-spanning-set.title: Spanning Set
def-spanning-set.html: If \(\Span(S) = V\), we say that \(S\) spans \(V\), or that \(S\) is a spanning set for \(V\).

def-subspace.title: Subspace
def-subspace.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). A subset \(W\) of \(V\) is called a subspace of \(V\), if \(W\) is also a vector space over \(F\) with addition and scalar multiplication inherited from \(V\).

def-sum-of-subspaces.title: Sum of Subspaces
def-sum-of-subspaces.html: Let \(W_1\), \(W_2\) be subspaces of a vector space \(V\). Then we define \[ W_1 + W_2 \coloneqq \left\{ \w_1 + \w_2 : \w_1 \in W_1 \text{ and } \w_2 \in W_2 \right\}. \]

def-vector-space.title: Vector Space
def-vector-space.html:
A set \(V\) over a field \(F\) with two operations: addition \(+\) and scalar multiplication \(\cdot\) \[ + : V \times V \to V, \quad \cdot : F \times V \to V \] such that satisfy the following axioms for all \(\v_1, \v_2, \v_3 \in V\) and \(\alpha, \beta \in F\):

  1. \(\v_1 + \v_2 = \v_2 + \v_1\)
  2. \((\v_1 + \v_2) + \v_3 = \v_1 + (\v_2 + \v_3)\)
  3. There exists \(\mathbf{0} \in V\) such that \(\v_1 + \mathbf{0} = \v_1\)
  4. There exists \(\v_1' \in V\) such that \(\v_1 + \v_1' = \mathbf{0}\)
  5. \(\alpha(\v_1 + \v_2) = \alpha\v_1 + \alpha\v_2\)
  6. \((\alpha+\beta)\v_1 = \alpha\v_1 + \beta\v_1\)
  7. \(\alpha(\beta\v_1) = (\alpha\beta)\v_1\)
  8. \(1\v_1 = \v_1\)

def-vectors-scalars.title: Vectors and Scalars
def-vectors-scalars.html:
Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). Then the elements of \(V\) are called vectors, and the elements of \(F\) are called scalars.

Additionally, \(\mathbf{0} \in V\) is called the zero vector, and \((\v_1')\) in (VS4) is called the inverse element of \(\v_1\).

exm-differentiable-functions.title: Differentiable Functions
exm-differentiable-functions.html:
Let \(C(\nR) = \{f : \nR \to \nR \mid f \text{ is continuous}\}\) be the set of all continuous functions on \(\nR\). We consider the set of differentiable functions: \[ D(\nR) = \{ f : \nR \to \nR \mid f \text{ is differentiable} \} \] To verify that \(D(\nR)\) is a subspace of \(C(\nR)\):

  • Subset: Since differentiability implies continuity, we have \(D(\nR) \subseteq C(\nR)\).
  • Zero vector: The zero function \(f(x) = 0\) is differentiable, so \(\mathbf{0} \in D(\nR)\).
  • Closure under addition: If \(f, g \in D(\nR)\), then \(f+g\) is differentiable with \((f+g)' = f' + g'\), so \(f+g \in D(\nR)\).
  • Closure under scalar multiplication: If \(f \in D(\nR)\) and \(c \in \nR\), then \(cf\) is differentiable with \((cf)' = c f'\), so \(cf \in D(\nR)\).

Thus, \(D(\nR)\) is a subspace of \(C(\nR)\).

exm-dimensions.title: Examples of Dimensions
exm-dimensions.html: \(\dim(F^n) = n\), \(\dim(F[x]_{\leq n}) = n+1\), and \(\dim(M_{m \times n}(F)) = mn\).

exm-direct-sum-of-matrix.html:
Consider the vector space \(V = M_n (\nC)\), and two of its subspaces:

  • \(W_1 = \{ \A \in M_n (\nC) : \A^{\top} = \A \}\) (the subspace of symmetric matrices);

  • \(W_2 = \{ \A \in M_n (\nC) : \A^{\top} = - \A \}\) (the subspace of skew-symmetric matrices).

We can derive that \(V = W_1 \oplus W_2\).

Proof. We first show that \(V = W_1 + W_2\). That is, any square matrix is a sum of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix. Let \(\A \in M_n (\nC)\), notice that we have the identity: \[ \A = \frac{1}{2} (\A + \A^{\top}) + \frac{1}{2} (\A - \A^{\top}) \] where the first term is symmetric and the second term is skew-symmetric. Therefore, any square matrix is a sum of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix.

To establish that \(W_1 \cap W_2 = \{ \O \}\), let \(\A \in W_1 \cap W_2\). By definition, this implies \(\A \in W_1\) and \(\A \in W_2\). Consequently, the identities \(\A = \A^{\top}\) and \(\A = - \A^{\top}\) must hold simultaneously. Substituting the former into the latter yields \(\A = - \A\). This implies \(2\A = \O\), and thus \(\A = \O\).

exm-line-not-subspace.title: Translated Line is Not a Subspace
exm-line-not-subspace.title_html: Translated Line is Not a Subspace
exm-line-not-subspace.html: \(W = \left\{ (x, y) \in \nR^2 : x + 2y = 3 \right\}\) is not a subspace of \(\nR^2\). This is because it does not contain the zero vector: \(0 + 2(0) = 0 \neq 3\), so \((0, 0) \notin W\).

exm-line-subspace.title: Line as Subspace
exm-line-subspace.html:
\(W = \left\{ (x, y) \in \nR^2 : x + 2y = 0 \right\}\) is a subspace of \(\nR^2\). Indeed:

  • Zero vector: \((0, 0) \in W\) since \(0 + 2(0) = 0\).
  • Addition: If \((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2) \in W\), then \((x_1+x_2) + 2(y_1+y_2) = (x_1+2y_1) + (x_2+2y_2) = 0 + 0 = 0\), so their sum is in \(W\).
  • Scalar multiplication: If \((x, y) \in W\) and \(c \in \nR\), then \((cx) + 2(cy) = c(x+2y) = c(0) = 0\), so \(c(x, y) \in W\).

exm-linear-combinations.title: Examples of Linear Combinations
exm-linear-combinations.html:
Below are some examples of linear combinations in different vector spaces:

  1. The vector \((2, 1, 0)\) in \(\nR^3\) is a linear combination of \(S = \{(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)\}\) because \[ (2, 1, 0) = -2 \cdot (1, 2, 3) + 1 \cdot (4, 5, 6). \]

  2. The polynomial \(f(x) = x^3 + 2x + 1\) in \(\mathbb{R}[x]\) is a linear combination of \(S = \{1, x, x^2, x^3\}\) because \[ f(x) = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot x + 0 \cdot x^2 + 1 \cdot x^3. \]

exm-linear-independence.title: Examples of Linear Independence
exm-linear-independence.html:
The following examples illustrate how to check for linear independence in various settings:

  1. Let \(S_1 = \{(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)\} \subseteq \nR^3\). To check linear independence, suppose \[ a(1, 2, 3) + b(4, 5, 6) = (0, 0, 0) \implies \begin{cases} a + 4b = 0 \\ 2a + 5b = 0 \\ 3a + 6b = 0 \end{cases} \] The first two equations give \(a = -4b\) and \(2(-4b) + 5b = 0 \implies -3b = 0\). Thus \(a = b = 0\), so \(S_1\) is linearly independent.

  2. Let \(S_2 = \{(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6), (7, 8, 9)\} \subseteq \nR^3\). Note that \[ (1, 2, 3) - 2(4, 5, 6) + (7, 8, 9) = (1-8+7, 2-10+8, 3-12+9) = (0, 0, 0). \] Since there exists a non-trivial solution, \(S_2\) is linearly dependent.

  3. Consider \(\{2x + 1, x^2 + 3\}\) in \(\nR[x]_{\leq 2}\). Suppose \[ a(2x + 1) + b(x^2 + 3) = 0 \implies bx^2 + 2ax + (a + 3b) = 0. \] Comparing coefficients of \(x^2, x, 1\), we have \(b = 0\), \(2a = 0\), and \(a + 3b = 0\). This implies \(a = b = 0\), so the set is linearly independent.

  4. Consider \(\{ \sin x, \cos x, e^x \}\) in \(D(\nR)\). Suppose for all \(x \in \nR\): \[ a \sin x + b \cos x + c e^x = 0. \] Setting \(x = 0\) gives \(b + c = 0\). Setting \(x = \pi\) gives \(-b + c e^\pi = 0\). Adding these gives \(c(1 + e^\pi) = 0\), so \(c = 0\) and hence \(b = 0\). Finally, setting \(x = \pi/2\) gives \(a + c e^{\pi/2} = 0 \implies a = 0\). Thus, the set is linearly independent.

exm-poly-degree-bound.title: Polynomials of Bounded Degree
exm-poly-degree-bound.html:
Let \(F[x]\) be the vector space of all polynomials over a field \(F\). For a fixed \(n \in \nN\), the set \(F[x]_{\leq n}\) of polynomials of degree at most \(n\) is a subspace of \(F[x]\).

  • Zero vector: The zero polynomial has degree \(-\infty\), so \(0 \in F[x]_{\leq n}\).
  • Addition: If \(\deg p \leq n\) and \(\deg q \leq n\), then \(\deg(p+q) \leq \max(\deg p, \deg q) \leq n\).
  • Scalar multiplication: If \(\deg p \leq n\) and \(c \in F\), then \(\deg(cp) \leq \deg p \leq n\).

exm-poly-exact-degree.title: Polynomials of Exact Degree
exm-poly-exact-degree.html:
The set \(F[x]_{=n}\) of polynomials of degree exactly \(n\) is not a subspace of \(F[x]\).

  • It does not contain the zero vector (since \(\deg 0 = -\infty \neq n\)).
  • It is not closed under addition. For example, if \(p(x) = x^n + x\) and \(q(x) = -x^n\), both have degree \(n\), but \(p(x) + q(x) = x\), which has degree \(1 \neq n\) (assuming \(n > 1\)).

exm-q-adjoin-sqrt2.title: \nQ Adjoin \sqrt{2}
exm-q-adjoin-sqrt2.html: Show that \(\nQ(\sqrt{2}) \coloneqq \left\{ a + b \sqrt{2} : a, b \in \nQ \right\}\) is a vector space over \(\nQ\) by checking all eight axioms.

exm-sifting.title: Sifting Example
exm-sifting.html:
Consider \(S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \v_3, \v_4, \v_5, \v_6 \}\) in \(\nR^3\) where: \[\begin{align*} \v_1 &= (1, 1, 1), & \v_2 &= (2, 2, 2), & \v_3 &= (1, 0, 0), \\ \v_4 &= (3, 2, 2), & \v_5 &= (1, 1, 0), & \v_6 &= (0, 0, 1). \end{align*}\]

We apply the sifting method:

  • \(\v_1 \neq \mathbf{0}\), so \(\v_1\) is kept.
  • \(\v_2 = 2\v_1\), so \(\v_2\) is removed.
  • \(\v_3\) is not a linear combination of \(\v_1\), so \(\v_3\) is kept.
  • \(\v_4 = 2\v_1 + 1\v_3\), so \(\v_4\) is removed.
  • Suppose \(\v_5 = a\v_1 + b\v_3\). Then \((1, 1, 0) = (a + b, a, a)\), which gives \(a = 0\) and \(a + b = 1\), so \(b = 1\). But then the second coordinate gives \(1 = a = 0\), which is a contradiction. So \(\v_5\) is not a linear combination of \(\v_1, \v_3\). Hence, \(\v_5\) is kept.
  • \(\v_6 = (0, 0, 1) = (1, 1, 1) - (1, 1, 0) = \v_1 - \v_5\), so \(\v_6\) is removed.

The sifted set is \(S' = \{ \v_1, \v_3, \v_5 \} = \{ (1, 1, 1), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0) \}\), which is linearly independent and spans the same space as \(S\).

exm-sifting-r2.title: Sifting in \nR^2
exm-sifting-r2.html:
Consider \(S = \{ (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1) \}\) in \(\nR^2\).

  • \((1, 0) \neq \mathbf{0}\), so \((1, 0)\) is kept.
  • \((0, 1) \notin \Span\{ (1, 0) \}\), so \((0, 1)\) is kept.
  • \((1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1) \in \Span\{ (1, 0), (0, 1) \}\), so \((1, 1)\) is removed.

The sifted set \(\{ (1, 0), (0, 1) \}\) is linearly independent and still spans \(\nR^2\).

exm-spanning-set.title: Spanning Set for Polynomials
exm-spanning-set.html: The set \(\{ 1, x, x^2 \}\) spans \(\nR[x]_{\leq 2}\), the space of polynomials of degree at most 2.

exm-standard-bases.title: Standard Bases
exm-standard-bases.html:
Commonly used standard bases for familiar vector spaces are listed below:

  • The standard basis for \(F^n\) is \(\{ \e_1, \e_2, \dots, \e_n \}\), where \(\e_i\) has a 1 in the \(i\)-th position and 0 elsewhere.
  • The standard basis for \(F[x]_{\leq n}\) is \(\{ 1, x, x^2, \dots, x^n \}\).
  • The standard basis for \(M_{m \times n}(F)\) is the set of matrices \(\E_{ij}\) having a 1 at entry \((i,j)\) and 0 elsewhere.

exm-symmetric-matrices.title: Symmetric Matrices
exm-symmetric-matrices.html:
The set of all symmetric matrices in \(M_n(F)\), denoted by \(S_n(F) = \{ \A \in M_n(F) : \A = \A^{\top} \}\), is a subspace of \(M_n(F)\).

  • Zero vector: The zero matrix \(\O\) is symmetric since \(\O^{\top} = \O\), so \(\O \in S_n(F)\).
  • Addition: If \(\A, \B \in S_n(F)\), then \((\A+\B)^{\top} = \A^{\top} + \B^{\top} = \A + \B\), so \(\A+\B \in S_n(F)\).
  • Scalar multiplication: If \(\A \in S_n(F)\) and \(c \in F\), then \((c\A)^{\top} = c\A^{\top} = c\A\), so \(c\A \in S_n(F)\).

exm-trace-free-matrices.title: Trace-free Matrices
exm-trace-free-matrices.html:
The set of all trace-free matrices in \(M_n(F)\), denoted by \(W = \{ \A \in M_n(F) : \tr(\A) = 0 \}\), is a subspace of \(M_n(F)\).

  • Zero vector: \(\tr(\O) = 0 + 0 + \cdots + 0 = 0\), so \(\O \in W\).
  • Addition: If \(\A, \B \in W\), then \(\tr(\A+\B) = \tr(\A) + \tr(\B) = 0 + 0 = 0\), so \(\A+\B \in W\).
  • Scalar multiplication: If \(\A \in W\) and \(c \in F\), then \(\tr(c\A) = c \tr(\A) = c(0) = 0\), so \(c\A \in W\).

exm-trivial-subspaces.title: Trivial Subspaces
exm-trivial-subspaces.html:
Given a vector space \(V\), then

  • \(V\) is a subspace of \(V\) itself;
  • \(\left\{ \mathbf{0} \right\}\) is a subspace of \(V\) (also known as the “zero subspace”);
  • \(\varnothing\) is not a subspace of \(V\).

exm-union-axes.title: Union of Axes
exm-union-axes.html:
Consider the vector space \(V = \nR^2\). Let \(W_1\) be the \(x\)-axis and \(W_2\) be the \(y\)-axis: \[ W_1 = \{ (x, 0) : x \in \nR \}, \quad W_2 = \{ (0, y) : y \in \nR \}. \] Both \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) are subspaces of \(\nR^2\). However, their union \(W_1 \cup W_2\) is not a subspace because it is not closed under addition.

Indeed, \((1, 0) \in W_1 \subseteq W_1 \cup W_2\) and \((0, 1) \in W_2 \subseteq W_1 \cup W_2\), but their sum: \[ (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) \] is not in \(W_1 \cup W_2\) since \((1, 1)\) is neither on the \(x\)-axis nor the \(y\)-axis.

exm-vector-spaces.title: Examples of Vector Spaces
exm-vector-spaces.html:
The following are classic examples of vector spaces:

  1. Most defaultly, \(F^n\) with the usual operations of \(+\) and \(\cdot\) is a vector space over \(F\).

  2. Working with polynomials is common too: \(F[x]\) with the usual operations of \(+\) and \(\cdot\) is a vector space over \(F\).

  3. Let \(\sD\) be any open interval. Let \[ C(\sD) \coloneqq \left\{ f: \sD \to \nR: f \text{ is continuous} \right\}. \] Then \(C(\sD)\) is a vector space over \(\nR\). The zero vector of this vector space is given by the zero function \((x \mapsto 0)\).

  4. Let \(F\) be any field and fix \(n \in \nN\). Then \(M_n(F)\) is a vector space over \(F\).

  5. The set \(V = \mathbb{R}_{>0}\) of positive real numbers forms a vector space over \(F = \mathbb{R}\) under the following operations: for \(x, y \in V\) and \(\alpha \in F\), define \[ x \oplus y \coloneqq xy, \quad \alpha \odot x \coloneqq x^\alpha = e^{\alpha \log x}. \] Under these operations, the zero vector is \(\mathbf{0} = 1\), and the additive inverse of \(x\) is \(x^{-1}\).

You can check if addition and scalar multiplication make sense and follow all axioms of vector spaces.

prp-union-subspaces.title: Union of Subspaces
prp-union-subspaces.html: Let \(W_1, W_2\) be subspaces of \(V\). Then \(W_1 \cup W_2\) is a subspace of \(V\) if and only if \(W_1 \subseteq W_2\) or \(W_2 \subseteq W_1\).

thm-basis-extension.title: Basis Extension Theorem
thm-basis-extension.html: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and \(S\) be a linearly independent subset of \(V\). Then \(S\) can be extended into a basis of \(V\).

thm-basis-theorem.title: Basis Theorem
thm-basis-theorem.html: If a vector space \(V\) over \(F\) has a finite basis, then every basis of \(V\) has the same number of vectors.

thm-dim-impl-eq.title: Dimension Implies Equality
thm-dim-impl-eq.html:
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over \(F\). If

  1. \(W \subseteq V\);
  2. \(\dim_F (W) = \dim_F (V)\),

then \(W = V\).

thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim.title: Dimension Formula of Subspace Sum
thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim.html: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space, and let \(W_1\), \(W_2\) subspaces of \(V\). Then \[ \dim(W_1 + W_2) = \dim (W_1) + \dim (W_2) - \dim(W_1 \cap W_2). \]

thm-intersection-subspaces.title: Intersection of Subspaces
thm-intersection-subspaces.html: Let \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) be subspaces of a vector space \(V\). Then the intersection \(W_1 \cap W_2\) is also a subspace of \(V\).

thm-inverse-unique.title: Additive Inverse is Unique
thm-inverse-unique.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). Then for every \(\v \in V\), its additive inverse described in (VS4), which is \(\v'\), is unique.

thm-left-cancellation.title: Left Cancellation Law
thm-left-cancellation.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\), let \(\u, \v_1, \v_2 \in V\). If \(\u + \v_1 = \u + \v_2\), then \(\v_1 = \v_2\).

thm-linear-dependence-lemma.title: Linear Dependence Lemma
thm-linear-dependence-lemma.html: \(\left\{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_m \right\}\) is linearly dependent if and only if either \(\v_1 = \mathbf{0}\) or for some \(r\), \(\v_r\) is a linear combination of \(\left\{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_{r - 1} \right\}\).

thm-maximal-indep.title: Maximal Independent Subset is a Basis
thm-maximal-indep.title_html: Maximal Independent Subset is a Basis
thm-maximal-indep.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space of dimension \(n\) over \(F\). Then any \(n\) independent vectors form a basis of \(V\). (We say that “any maximal linearly independent subset forms a basis”).

thm-negation-scalar.title: Negation as Scalar Multiplication
thm-negation-scalar.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) and \(\v \in V\) be any vector. Then \(-\v = (-1) \cdot \v\).

thm-negative-scalar-dist.title: Negative Scalar Distribution
thm-negative-scalar-dist.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). For any \(\alpha \in F\) and \(\v \in V\), we have \((-\alpha)\v = -(\alpha\v)\).

thm-right-cancellation.title: Right Cancellation Law
thm-right-cancellation.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\), let \(\u, \v_1, \v_2 \in V\). If \(\v_1 + \u = \v_2 + \u\), then \(\v_1 = \v_2\).

thm-scalar-zero-vector.title: Scalar Multiplication by Zero Vector
thm-scalar-zero-vector.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). For any scalar \(\alpha \in F\), we have \(\alpha\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}\).

thm-sift.title: Sifting Method
thm-sift.html:
Let \(S = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_m \}\) be a subset of \(V\). Then there exists a subset \(S' \subseteq S\) such that:

  1. \(S'\) is linearly independent, and
  2. \(\Span(S') = \Span(S)\).

thm-size-bounds.title: Size Bounds for Independent and Spanning Sets
thm-size-bounds.title_html: Size Bounds for Independent and Spanning Sets
thm-size-bounds.html:
Let \(V\) be a vector space of dimension \(n\) over \(F\), and \(S \subseteq V\) be a subset.

  1. If \(|S| > n\), then \(S\) cannot be linearly independent.
  2. If \(|S| < n\), then \(S\) cannot span \(V\).

thm-span-preservation.title: Span Preservation
thm-span-preservation.html: Let \(S = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m, \w \} \subseteq V\). If \(\w \in \Span \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m \}\), then \[ \Span(S) = \Span \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_m \}. \]

thm-span-subspace.title: Spanning Set as Subspace
thm-span-subspace.html: The span of any subset \(S \subseteq V\) is a subspace of \(V\). Moreover, it is the smallest subspace of \(V\) containing \(S\).

thm-steinitz.title: Steinitz Exchange/Replacement Theorem
thm-steinitz.html:
Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). Suppose:

  • \(G = \{ \v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n \}\) spans \(V\);
  • \(L = \{ \u_1, \u_2, \dots, \u_m \}\) is linearly independent.

Then \(m \leq n\).

thm-subapce-sum-theorem.title: Sum of Subspaces Theorem
thm-subapce-sum-theorem.html: \(W_1 + W_2\) is a subspace of \(V\). Furthermore, this is the smallest subspace containing both \(W_1\) and \(W_2\).

thm-subspace-test.title: Subspace Test
thm-subspace-test.html:
Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\) and \(W \subseteq V\). Then \(W\) is a subspace of \(V\) if and only if the following are satisfied:

  • \(W\) is non-empty;
  • \(W\) is closed under addition: \(\w_1 + \w_2 \in W\) for all \(\w_1, \w_2 \in W\);
  • \(W\) is closed under scalar multiplication: \(\alpha \w \in W\) for all \(\alpha \in F\) and \(\w \in W\).

thm-unique-representation.title: Unique Representation
thm-unique-representation.html: Let \(B = \{ \v_1, \dots, \v_n \}\) be a basis for \(V\). Then every vector \(\v \in V\) can be written as a linear combination of elements in \(B\) in exactly one way.

thm-zero-product.title: Zero Product Law
thm-zero-product.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\), \(\v \in V\), and \(\alpha \in F\). If \(\alpha\v = \mathbf{0}\), then either \(\alpha = 0\) or \(\v = \mathbf{0}\).

thm-zero-scalar-mult.title: Zero Scalar Annihilates
thm-zero-scalar-mult.html: Let \(\v \in V\) for a vector space \(V\) over \(F\). Then \(0 \cdot \v = \mathbf{0}\).

thm-zero-unique.title: Zero Vector is Unique
thm-zero-unique.html: Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(F\). The zero vector \(\mathbf{0} \in V\) is unique.
